Coarsening to 5 days has a marked influence on interfacial orientation, as seen in Figure 8. Perhaps most evident in this figure is the narrower distribution of orientations, which would be expected for a more regular arrangement of solid dendrites. There remain two significant density peaks parallel to the x-y plane. However, these normals are distributed less uniformly after the lengthened coarsening process. The two peaks in Figure 8 are separated by a measure of π about the growth direction. In this respect, it can be visualized that for each normal vector projected from an interfacial patch, there exists a complimentary vector, 180° away in almost perfect two-fold symmetry. Such an orientation proposes an elevated density of shapes exhibiting high relative uniformity in the growth direction (z-axis) with respect to the x- and y-axes. This stereographic projection is typical of the planar shape in Figure 9, where each surface yields its distinct peak complemented by another peak from the parallel surface in the opposite direction.

In addition to directionality assessment, computational analysis using IDL software can determine curvature distributions and mode interfacial shapes. Alkemper and Voorhees have previously generated plots that display H and K distributions independently, illustrating the distribution of the curvatures within the microstructure.⁵ Additionally, Mendoza's previous curvature analysis has identified key parameters of curvature that dictate the morphology of the interface. If H is positive, the interface has a solid spherical shape, while a negative H represents a liquid spherical shape.² Moreover, Mendoza's analysis determined that if a point on the interface has a positive Gaussian curvature, the concavity of the interface is determined by the sign of H. If H is positive, the interface is concave towards the solid, while if H is negative, it is convex towards the solid. Additionally, an interface with K=0 has a cylindrical interface composed of solid (if H is positive) or liquid (if H is negative). Interestingly, saddle-shaped interfaces are characterized by negative Gaussian curvatures.² Thus, the sign of the mean curvature determines the dominant principle curvature. Figure 10 graphically illustrates these curvature criteria.
